Recognise function-verb constructions: a noun that carries the meaning + an “empty” verb (nehmen, bringen, kommen, stehen, ziehen).
Replace them with the simple verb: Abschied nehmen = sich verabschieden; zum Ausdruck bringen = ausdrücken.

Write a condolence card in German.
It's February 2034. Friedrich Mertens has died peacefully in his sleep, at the age of 99. Lena wants to write Grete a condolence card and asks Ludwig for help.
Grandpa, I want to write Grete a card. But everything I write sounds wrong. How do you write something like that in German?
In German there are fixed formulas for it. They're a bit stiff, but they help. Start with: “Dear Grete, it was with great sadness that we learned of Friedrich's death.”
You can say that. In writing, people often say: “We would like to express our sincere condolences.” Or: “We share in your grief with all our hearts.”
“Anteil nehmen”. That's an expression like “Abschied nehmen”, isn't it?
Exactly. A function-verb construction, as your grandmother used to say. The verb says almost nothing, the noun says everything. “Abschied nehmen” sounds more solemn than “sich verabschieden”.
Can I write something personal too? That he always sat by the window and listened?
Absolutely. The formulas are only the frame. The picture inside it, you have to paint yourself. Write: “We will remember him as the silent listener by the window.”
And at the end? He waited sixty-nine years for her. And then he only had four years with her.
Then write what he would have said himself: “His greatest wish came true. He was allowed to be by your side.” Nothing more is needed.
And the signature? “Yours faithfully” really doesn't fit.
No. You write: “In silent mourning” or “With deep affection”. Or simply: “We are here for you.” That's the most important sentence. And it isn't a function-verb construction.
“Anteil nehmen an” = to share in (someone's grief)
“Abschied nehmen” = to say goodbye, to take one's leave
“in Erinnerung behalten” = to remember, to keep in one's memory

In chapter 45 you learned the first expressions (eine Entscheidung treffen, Hilfe leisten). At B2 many more turn up, especially in formal writing. The structure: noun (the meaning) + a “weakened” verb (nehmen, bringen, kommen, stehen, ziehen, gehen, finden).
Abschied nehmen, Anteil nehmen, Rücksicht nehmen, Stellung nehmen (to take a position)
zum Ausdruck bringen, in Ordnung bringen, zur Sprache bringen (to bring up, to raise)
zur Ruhe kommen, in Frage kommen, zur Sprache kommen, ums Leben kommen (to lose one's life)
zur Verfügung stehen, unter Druck stehen, in Kontakt stehen
in Erfüllung gehen, zu Ende gehen, in Rente gehen
in Betracht ziehen, zur Verantwortung ziehen (to hold responsible)
The constructions with “kommen” and “gehen” are often passive or intransitive (something happens): “Das Thema kam zur Sprache” = the subject was brought up.
Mit großer Trauer haben wir vom Tod … erfahren.
Wir möchten dir / Ihnen unser herzliches Beileid aussprechen.
Wir nehmen von Herzen Anteil an deiner / Ihrer Trauer.
Wir werden ihn / sie als … in Erinnerung behalten.
Wenn du etwas brauchst, sind wir für dich da.
In stiller Trauer / In tiefer Verbundenheit / Mit stillem Gruß
Never end a condolence card with “Mit freundlichen Grüßen” or “Liebe Grüße”. And avoid “Ich weiß, wie du dich fühlst” — Germans prefer discretion.

In everyday speech, function-verb constructions can sound pompous. “Ich nehme jetzt Abschied” at a friend's door sounds odd; you say “Tschüss!” or “Ich gehe jetzt”. At a funeral, in a speech or a letter, though, they are exactly the right register.
I would like to express my condolences.
Many people shared in her grief.
After the ceremony she finally found peace.
We are at your disposal at any time.

Friedrich Mertens died on the night of the eleventh to the twelfth of February 2034, at the age of ninety-nine, peacefully, in his sleep, in his room at the “Am Kollwitzpark” care home. The night nurse found him at six in the morning. He was lying on his back, his hands folded on the duvet, and on the bedside table next to him lay his glasses, an old watch and a yellowed photograph of a young woman at the piano with a bouquet of white lilac. On the back, someone had written long ago, in pencil: “Konzerthaus, May 1960. For F.”

Mara found out at half past six, on her way to work, on the U2 platform. The director of the home, Mrs Petersen, called her because Friedrich, without telling anyone, had given Mara's number as his second emergency contact, after Sophie in Lübeck. Mara didn't get on the train. She called her ward and said she'd be late today, for the first time in her life without an explanation. Then she walked to Kollwitzpark through the cold, dark streets and thought about the promise she had made a year earlier, on ward 4, at Grete's bedside.

The home was quiet when she arrived. The carers walked more slowly than usual down the corridor. In front of Friedrich's door there was a small candle on the floor, lit by the night nurse, as was the custom at the home when someone died. Mrs Petersen came to meet her, took her hand and said only: “Last night he was still laughing. Mrs Hoffmann read to him from the newspaper and he laughed at a misprint. Then he went to bed.” Mara nodded. It was a good last evening, she thought. A laugh at a misprint. That suited him.

Grete was sitting in her room by the window, already dressed, in her grey cardigan, her hair combed. She had found out at six, from the night nurse. She hadn't cried. She had washed, dressed and combed her hair, like every morning, and sat down by the window, like every morning, and was looking out at the park, where it was still dark. When Mara came in, she turned round and said, in a very calm voice: “Mara, child. You shouldn't have come. You're on shift, after all. I'm fine.” And Mara remembered what Friedrich had said in December: she'll pretend everything is all right. That's what she always does.

Mara said nothing. She took off her coat, put it on the chair and sat down next to Grete by the window. She took her hand, the thin old hand with the long fingers that had played the piano for ninety years, and held it tight. Outside it was slowly getting light. A blackbird began to sing in the bare tree in front of the window. And after a long time, maybe ten minutes, maybe half an hour, Grete said quietly, without looking at Mara: “Sixty-nine years I waited for him. And then I had only four.” And then she cried. For the first time since Mara had known her.

Sophie came from Lübeck in the afternoon, by train, with red eyes and a small suitcase. She brought an envelope her grandfather had given her in the autumn, “just in case”. Inside was his last wish, on a single page, in his neat, old-fashioned handwriting. He wanted no church and no priest. He wanted a small ceremony in the common room of the home, where he had sat by the window every Wednesday. He wanted Grete to play, if she could, and if she couldn't, then nobody should play. And he wanted part of his ashes to be scattered in the Baltic Sea at Travemünde, where the Trave flows into the sea, in front of the house where he had waited sixty-nine years for her.

And then, right at the bottom, there was one more sentence, in a different pen, apparently added later. Sophie read it aloud, her voice trembling, in Grete's room, where Mara, Ludwig and Lena were now sitting too: “And for Mara Ionescu: thank you for keeping your promise before it was due. Please keep it from now on as well. She won't admit it. But she needs you.” Mara couldn't answer. Grete looked at her for a long time, then said, with her old ironic look, which had reappeared through the tears: “Typical Friedrich. Silent for sixty-nine years, and then he writes everything down.”

In the days that followed, condolence cards arrived at the home, dozens of them. From the residents, from the carers, from the whole of Kastanienallee. Elif wrote one in coloured pencils, with a drawing of a window and an armchair in front of it. Readers of the Berliner Zeitung, who knew Friedrich from Katrin Krüger's article, sent letters from all over Germany. And Lena brought the card she had written with Ludwig's help, with the fixed formulas and the picture inside them. Grete read them all, a few every evening, with her magnifying glass, in her armchair. She said nothing about them. But she put every card in the old tin box where her sheet music from 1956 had once been kept.

The ceremony took place ten days later, on a cold, clear Wednesday afternoon, at four o'clock. At the time when Elif and Ayşe would otherwise come for the lesson. The common room was full: the residents of the home, the carers, the whole of Kastanienallee, Susanne and Peter from Hanover, Mirko from Dresden, Thomas with Anja, Katrin Krüger from the Berliner Zeitung, who wasn't taking notes. By the window, in Friedrich's place, stood his armchair, empty, with a small bouquet of white lilac on it, which Ludwig had got from a florist in Mitte, because in February there was no white lilac anywhere else.
Outside, in front of the window, it began to snow gently as the ceremony began.

Ludwig gave a short speech. He wasn't a good speaker and he knew it, but Grete had asked him. He said he had known Friedrich for only four years, but in those four years he had learned from him the most important thing a man can learn: how to wait. Not impatiently. Not bitterly. But the way you wait for a tram that you know is coming, even if the timetable doesn't match. “Friedrich waited sixty-nine years,” said Ludwig. “And when it came, he got on. And he rode with her to the end of the line.” Then he sat down, nobody said anything, and all you could hear was the ticking of the clock on the wall.

Then Grete stood up. She walked slowly, without help, to the piano. Elif wanted to jump up to help her, but her mother held her back. Grete sat down, adjusted the stool, as she had for ninety years, and took out of her bag the old metronome she had given Elif in December and that Elif had brought back to her that morning, “just for today”. She put it on the piano and set the pendulum going. Tick. Tock. And then she played the Brahms sonata she had played in 1960 at the Konzerthaus for a young man sitting in the twelfth row with a bouquet of lilac he hadn't had the courage to give her.

She played more softly than ever. Her hands were trembling. Twice she stopped, in the middle of a bar, and the whole room held its breath. But the metronome went on ticking, calmly, without fear, as Mr Wendland had promised in 1943 in the cellar, and each time her fingers found their way back. When she played the last chord, very softly, she didn't look at the keys, but at the window, at the empty armchair with the lilac. And she said, so quietly that only Mara, who was sitting closest, heard: “There, Friedrich. Now you've heard it to the end.”

After the ceremony the guests stayed on for a long time, over coffee and Andrei's cake, and told each other stories about Friedrich. How he brought the newspaper every Wednesday and never read it. How he once tried to teach Elif to play chess and gave up after three games because she won every time. How he cried at Grete's birthday in May in his oldest suit, without being ashamed. Mr Petrowski from room 14, who had been speaking again since December, said a single sentence, but everyone listened: “He said good morning to me every morning. Three years. Even when I didn't answer.”

In the evening, when everyone had left, Mara stayed with Grete. She stayed the next evening too, and the one after that. She no longer brought the newspaper, because there was no one left not to read it. She brought tea and cake from Lena's café, and sometimes they said nothing to each other for a whole hour, and at other times Grete told stories from 1957 that she had never told anyone. On the third evening, when Mara wanted to leave, Grete held her by the arm, as Friedrich had done in December. “Mara,” she said. “Wednesday at four. Tell Elif and her mother to be on time. The lesson isn't cancelled.” Mara smiled, for the first time in a week. Friedrich had been right. She never admitted that she needed anyone. But she never stopped either.
